Did you know?

A Grand National winner visited The Hawthorns.

Red Rum was a special guest at John Osborne’s testimonial in May 1978. A memorable night, even before the football began.

Let Baggie Bird show you the story →

Albion’s title once fitted in a pocket.

A matchbox cover celebrated the 1920 championship with stripes and a team photograph. A tiny object with a big story.

Open the championship matchbox →

Not every goalkeeper wore a different shirt.

Joe Reader’s surviving kit is believed to date from 1900/01. Like his teammates, he wore stripes — with long trousers.

Look at the keeper’s kit →

The song thrush has a familiar local name.

A throstle is a song thrush. Hawthorn trees, its favoured habitat, inspired the ground’s name and feature with the bird in Albion’s crest.

1878–1900

From the works to the league.

A team formed by young factory workers becomes a cup-winning club and a founder of the Football League. Before The Hawthorns, there is Stoney Lane.

It starts at the spring works. ↗Third time lucky at the Oval. ↗Billy Bassett, a lifetime of Albion. ↗

1901–1939

The champions & the double.

A new ground, the fight to keep the club alive, a league championship and a remarkable combination of promotion and the FA Cup.

Champions of England. ↗The other kind of double. ↗A championship in your pocket. ↗

1940–1968

A habit of winning cups.

Allen and Barlow set the standard in the 1950s. Brown and Astle carry it forward. Two decades leave three major cups and a host of Albion heroes.

Five goals and a fourth FA Cup. ↗A final won at home. ↗One goal that never gets old. ↗

1969–1984

Football that broke barriers.

Regis, Cunningham and Batson shine in an attacking side and confront racism. Their impact changes far more than the league table.

Cyrille Regis, a force for change. ↗Laurie Cunningham, in full flight. ↗Brendon Batson, part of the breakthrough. ↗

1985–2001

The long road back.

Years away from the top flight bring setbacks and new heroes. At Wembley in 1993, a play-off win offers a way out of the third tier.

Wembley points the way back. ↗“Super Bob” Taylor. ↗

2002–2020

Hope. Nerves. Albion.

The Premier League return, an impossible-looking escape, a Championship title and promotion in a season interrupted by a pandemic.

1878 · It starts at the spring works.

Stories · 1878

It starts at the spring works.

Young workers, a football and the beginning of Albion.

The club that became West Bromwich Albion was formed in 1878 by young workers at George Salter’s spring factory. Its first identity was West Bromwich Strollers; the Albion name followed.

The club’s own history presents the walk to Wednesbury to buy a ball as a legend, rather than an established record. What is certain is how quickly the team grew: within a decade, Albion were FA Cup winners and members of the new Football League.

Matches · 1888

Third time lucky at the Oval.

A first FA Cup, before Wembley became the final’s home.

Albion2–1Preston

After defeats in the 1886 and 1887 finals, Albion finally lifted the FA Cup in 1888, beating Preston North End 2–1. The winning side belongs to the era of the Oval, long before Wembley became part of cup-final tradition.

That same year, Albion joined the 12 founder members of the Football League. The cup-winning photograph captures a team standing at the beginning of both the club’s trophy story and the league game familiar to supporters today.

Objects · 1888

The faces in the first cup photograph.

Look closely at the photograph that opens this museum.

A posed team photograph can make the distant past unexpectedly close. Albion’s 1888 players appear in striped shirts, with the formal posture and arrangements familiar from Victorian group portraits.

This surviving image is catalogued by Wikimedia Commons as the 1888 team. The photographer is unknown. Enlarge it and look at the individual faces, the clothing and the differences from a modern squad photograph. It is an archival photograph, rather than a modern reconstruction.

Matches · 1892

A second cup. A familiar rival.

Albion beat Aston Villa 3–0 in the FA Cup final.

Albion3–0Aston Villa

Albion’s second FA Cup arrived in 1892 with a 3–0 win over Aston Villa. The two clubs were already regular opponents on football’s biggest stage: Villa had beaten Albion in the 1887 final and would do so again in 1895.

The photograph of the 1892 winners gives another view of the club’s Victorian cup sides. These were Stoney Lane years, before a move to The Hawthorns changed the setting of Albion’s story.

People · 1880s–1930s

Billy Bassett, a lifetime of Albion.

From cup-winning winger to the chairman’s seat.

Billy Bassett was part of Albion’s cup-winning sides before becoming a shareholder, director and chairman. The club’s account of its 1898 film footage notes that his service eventually stretched beyond 50 years.

His story connects the playing field to the survival of the institution. In the early twentieth century, Bassett worked alongside Fred Everiss as Albion faced severe financial trouble. The familiar club name endured because people kept it going between the famous Saturdays.

Objects · 24 September 1898

When the stripes began to move.

Albion on film at Ewood Park in 1898.

A short surviving film shows Albion playing Blackburn Rovers at Ewood Park on 24 September 1898. The club shared the footage in 2014 with the help of the North West Film Archive.

Albion lost 4–1, but the film’s appeal lies beyond the result. It lets supporters see a team from the nineteenth century moving on a pitch rather than standing for a portrait. Billy Bassett was in his final season as a player; Ben Garfield scored Albion’s goal. The source page links to the archive film.

Places · 1885–1900

Before The Hawthorns: Stoney Lane.

The ground Albion left, with an emphatic farewell.

Stoney Lane was the setting for Albion’s late-Victorian years, including the cup-winning era of 1888 and 1892. The move to The Hawthorns in 1900 marked the end of that chapter.

The final season there ended with an 8–0 home victory over Nottingham Forest. The club’s archive records 199 senior Albion games at Stoney Lane, with 113 wins. Looking back beyond the current ground is a reminder that even a football club’s most familiar traditions once had another home.

Places · 3 September 1900

The day The Hawthorns opened.

Four months of construction. More than a century of memories.

Albion1–1Derby County

The Hawthorns opened on 3 September 1900 after construction lasting just four months. The first fixture ended 1–1 against Derby County. Steve Bloomer scored for Derby; Chippy Simmons equalised for Albion.

The club initially held a lease and bought the freehold in 1913. Hawthorn bushes had grown on the estate, giving the new ground a name that became part of Albion’s identity. Today’s ground looks very different, but the site has carried the club’s home matches since that opening afternoon.

Objects · Believed to be 1900/01

Joe Reader’s long trousers.

A goalkeeper in stripes, before the modern keeper’s kit.

The club’s archive documents surviving garments believed to have been worn by goalkeeper Joe Reader during the 1900/01 season. The dating is an attribution in the source, rather than a certainty.

Reader wore blue and white stripes like his teammates, with long trousers helping to distinguish him. Goalkeepers of the period could be identified by caps or different socks and shorts, before a separate shirt became the familiar convention. The original kit is shown on the linked club page; the graphic here is a catalogue symbol, not a photograph or replica.

People · From 1902

Fred Everiss, keeping Albion alive.

The work behind the victories.

Fred Everiss became Albion’s secretary-manager in 1902, in an era when administration and running the team were closely bound together. The club’s retrospective describes financial crises, the loss of a stand to fire and repeated efforts to keep the business afloat.

Everiss and Billy Bassett helped carry Albion through those difficulties. It is easy for a history to move directly between trophies; his story explains some of the work required for the club to survive long enough to win them.

Objects · 2 September 1905

A programme with a purpose.

Albion News began as a way to help the club survive.

The club traces the birth of The Albion News & Official Programme to the opening home match of the 1905 season, against Burnley. It followed a period of serious financial pressure and the destruction of the old “Noah’s Ark” stand by fire.

The programme offered a regular new source of income. That origin gives a familiar matchday object a different meaning: something bought to read before kick-off was also part of an effort to sustain the club. The type treatment here is a modern interpretation, not a scan of the 1905 issue.

Objects · 1912

An album has room for the defeats.

The 1912 finalists, preserved in a team portrait.

This photograph records the Albion team who reached the FA Cup final in 1912. They were beaten by Barnsley after a replay, a reminder that a long cup tradition includes disappointments as well as winning days.

The image sits between the Victorian winners and the champions of 1920. Compare the faces, shirts and formal arrangement with the other team photographs in the collection. The photographer is unknown; the image survives in the public domain.

1919/20 · Champions of England.
← Back to the collectionALBION / 013

Stories · 1919/20

Champions of England.

104 goals. 60 points. The title belongs to Albion.

When league football returned after the First World War, Albion produced an extraordinary season. They won the First Division in 1919/20 with 28 victories, 104 goals and 60 points, at a time when a win was worth two points.

The title was secured with four games still to play. Fred Morris led the goalscoring, while the defensive foundations included Jesse Pennington, Joe Smith and goalkeeper Hubert Pearson. The photograph shows the team with the league trophy and the Charity Shield won later in 1920.

People · 1919/20

Fred Morris, finding the net.

The goals at the heart of a title-winning season.

Fred Morris scored 37 league goals in Albion’s championship season of 1919/20. He became the first Albion player to pass 30 in a league campaign and finished as the First Division’s leading scorer.

Five of his goals came in an 8–0 victory over Notts County. His record belongs within a team story rather than apart from it: the championship combined prolific scoring with an experienced defence. Open the team photograph to see the men behind the figures.

Objects · 1920

A championship in your pocket.

An everyday object becomes a tiny piece of football history.

A commemorative matchbox cover in the club’s archive celebrates Albion’s 1920 championship. Produced by Glossoids of London, it carries blue and white stripes, championship wording and a team photograph.

The club historian draws attention to the photograph’s setting in front of the Halfords Lane stand, suggesting an image different from the more familiar champions’ portrait. Such small objects can preserve evidence that larger accounts miss. The linked source shows the actual cover; this museum’s graphic is a modern interpretation.

Stories · 1930/31

The other kind of double.

The FA Cup and promotion, in one remarkable season.

Albion’s 1930/31 side combined an FA Cup triumph with promotion from the Second Division. They had to manage a long cup run while chasing one of only two promotion places.

The cup campaign included replays and a semi-final against Everton. After winning at Wembley, Albion still had league business to finish. Victories over Stoke and Charlton completed promotion. The achievement links two very different kinds of pressure: the single match that wins a trophy and the season-long work that moves a club up a division.

People · 25 April 1931

W.G. Richardson, twice at Wembley.

Two goals put the cup in Albion hands.

Albion2–1Birmingham

W.G. Richardson scored both Albion goals in the 1931 FA Cup final, a 2–1 victory over Birmingham. Captain Tommy Glidden received the trophy at Wembley.

The celebrations continued after promotion was secured. On 11 May, the Prince of Wales visited The Hawthorns to meet the team. The club’s account connects Richardson, Glidden, chairman Billy Bassett and a season whose achievement reached beyond the result of the final alone.

Matches · 1 May 1954

Five goals and a fourth FA Cup.

Albion 3, Preston North End 2.

Albion3–2Preston

Albion’s 1953/54 side came close to a league and cup double. They finished second in the First Division and ended the season with the FA Cup after a 3–2 victory over Preston North End.

The Wembley win belonged to a side built around players such as Ronnie Allen, Ray Barlow and captain Len Millard. It was the fourth FA Cup in Albion’s history. Read the club historian’s retrospective for the injuries, selection difficulties and attacking football behind that short line in the honours list.

People · The 1954 cup side

Ronnie Allen, the complete forward.

At the centre of one of Albion’s finest attacks.

Ronnie Allen was central to the attacking strength of the 1954 cup-winning side. In the Wembley final, George Lee supplied the ball for Allen to open the scoring against Preston.

The club’s detailed match account places him alongside Frank Griffin, Paddy Ryan, Johnnie Nicholls and Lee in a forward line that had scored 85 goals between them that season. His story is a useful way into that team: begin with a familiar cup result, then look at the combinations and players that made it possible.

People · The 1950s

Ray Barlow, making the game flow.

The passer in the heart of the 1954 team.

Ray Barlow’s partnership with Ronnie Allen runs through the club’s accounts of its celebrated 1950s side. Barlow helped shape Albion’s attacking play and, alongside Len Millard, contain Preston’s Tom Finney in the 1954 final.

He later succeeded Millard as captain and led Albion on their 1957 visit to the Soviet Union. The club’s tribute remembers a player whose influence was expressed in passing and judgement, qualities that a goals column cannot capture.

The League Cup, before the Wembley final.

Albion5–3West HamAggregate score across two legs

Albion won the League Cup in 1966, when the final was still played over two legs. The opponents were West Ham, a side featuring Bobby Moore, Martin Peters and Geoff Hurst.

The route included wins over Walsall, Leeds, Coventry and Aston Villa, followed by a two-legged semi-final against Peterborough. Albion emerged from the final with a 5–3 aggregate victory. It was a major trophy celebrated at The Hawthorns, before the competition’s final moved to Wembley the following year.

People · 1964–1974 at Albion

Jeff Astle. The King.

174 goals, and one finish remembered above all.

Jeff Astle scored 174 goals in 361 Albion appearances. His 1968 FA Cup campaign included a goal in every round and the extra-time winner against Everton in the final.

The club’s profile remembers both a prolific centre-forward and a personality closely bound to West Bromwich. His place in the club’s memory is visible beyond the records: the Astle Gates turn the walk to the ground into a meeting with its past.

Matches · 18 May 1968

One goal that never gets old.

Astle settles the FA Cup final in extra time.

Albion1–0EvertonAfter extra time · Wembley

The 1968 final ended goalless after 90 minutes. In extra time, Jeff Astle’s left-footed strike beat Gordon West and put Albion ahead. The score stayed 1–0.

The fifth FA Cup was won by a side including Tony Brown, Bobby Hope, Graham Williams and goalkeeper John Osborne, managed by Alan Ashman. The goal completed Astle’s remarkable run of scoring in every round. The cup belongs to the whole team; its defining image remains the centre-forward who found the finish.

People · 1963–1980: first-team career

Tony Brown, the record that endures.

720 appearances. 279 goals. Bomber.

Tony Brown is Albion’s record appearance maker and goalscorer, with 720 appearances and 279 goals. His first-team career stretched from 1963 to 1980, linking the cup-winning 1960s to the attacking side of the late 1970s.

That span makes him a thread through several rooms of this museum. He won the League Cup in 1966 and the FA Cup in 1968, then played alongside a new generation including Cyrille Regis and Laurie Cunningham. Following one player can reveal how teams and eras overlap.

People · Joined Albion in 1977

Cyrille Regis, a force for change.

A centre-forward whose influence travelled beyond football.

Cyrille Regis arrived at Albion from Hayes in 1977. His rise from non-league football made him a central figure in a side remembered for its attacking quality and ambition.

At Albion, his friendship with Laurie Cunningham and Brendon Batson developed alongside their experiences as prominent Black players confronting racism. The club’s profile places the football and the personal story together. His later recognition in the National Football Museum’s Hall of Fame reflects an influence that cannot be reduced to goals.

People · Albion’s late-1970s side

Laurie Cunningham, in full flight.

Skill, speed and courage on the wing.

Laurie Cunningham came to Albion from Orient and became one of the most exciting players in the late-1970s team. The club’s tribute singles out his UEFA Cup performance against Valencia as a defining display.

His brilliance existed alongside the racist abuse he and other Black players faced. The same account remembers the support he shared with Cyrille Regis and Brendon Batson. Cunningham later moved to Real Madrid; his Albion years remain central to the way the club remembers both its football and its role in challenging prejudice.

People · Joined Albion in 1978

Brendon Batson, part of the breakthrough.

The full-back in an adventurous Albion side.

Brendon Batson followed Ron Atkinson from Cambridge United to Albion in 1978. The club’s retrospective describes how he and Derek Statham, on the opposite flank, were encouraged to overlap and support the attack.

Alongside Cyrille Regis and Laurie Cunningham, he became part of a group whose prominence challenged assumptions about Black footballers. Remembering him only through that shared legacy misses the player: a key defender in a side committed to going forward. Injury eventually cut short his playing career.

Stories · The late 1970s and beyond

More than the “Three Degrees”.

Three distinct players. A shared place in the game’s history.

Cyrille Regis, Laurie Cunningham and Brendon Batson became widely known by the nickname “The Three Degrees”. Their impact came through their football, their visibility and their response to the racism directed at them.

The National Football Museum inducted Regis into its Hall of Fame in 2019. Albion’s account connects that recognition to the pioneering role of all three. Their stories deserve to be read individually as well as together: a striker, a winger and a full-back whose lives and influence extended well beyond a single team photograph.

Stories · 1978/79

The team that made people look.

A title challenge, European nights and a side full of invention.

Albion entered 1979 on the back of wins at Arsenal and Manchester United and briefly topped the First Division in January. The campaign eventually brought third place and a UEFA Cup quarter-final appearance.

The club historian’s retrospective asks how close that side came to something greater. It also traces how quickly the group changed: Cunningham and Len Cantello left, followed later by Ron Atkinson, Bryan Robson and Remi Moses. The season remains compelling partly because the team’s promise and its impermanence sit side by side.

Objects · May 1978

The night Red Rum came to football.

John Osborne’s testimonial had an unusual guest.

Goalkeeper John Osborne’s testimonial in May 1978 included a visit from Red Rum, the three-time Grand National winner. The club’s archive preserves both a programme and a ticket from the occasion.

The appearance was arranged to help draw a crowd for a long-serving player’s benefit. It is a reminder of the variety contained in a club archive: not every item records a title race or a cup final. The ticket-like graphic here is a modern interpretation; the actual surviving objects appear on the linked club page.

Matches · 1993

Wembley points the way back.

A 3–0 play-off final win over Port Vale.

Albion3–0Port Vale

Albion’s 1993 play-off final victory over Port Vale lifted the club out of the third tier. It followed a memorable semi-final against Swansea and gave supporters a Wembley success in a difficult period of the club’s history.

Ossie Ardiles’ side offered a new set of names to remember, including Bob Taylor, Andy Hunt, Ian Hamilton and Kevin Donovan. The club later marked the occasion’s 25th anniversary with the full match and a book of interviews, preserving the season as more than a single scoreline.

People · The 1990s and the return

“Super Bob” Taylor.

A goalscorer for the rebuilding years.

Bob Taylor became one of the faces of Albion’s route back from the third tier. The club’s Legend Days profile places him at the heart of the goalscoring story of the 1990s.

His Albion career also included a return that mattered at the other end of the table: five goals in eight matches helped the club avoid relegation, with Taylor scoring in a final-day 2–0 win over champions Charlton. It is the sort of contribution that explains why a player stays in supporters’ affections long after the match reports have faded.

Stories · 2001/02

The wait for the top flight ends.

Albion reach the Premier League for the first time.

Automatic promotion in 2002 ended Albion’s 16-year absence from the top flight. Gary Megson’s team had turned a long period of second-tier struggle into a return to the highest division.

Darren Moore scored the opener in the decisive 2–0 home win over Crystal Palace. His first season at the club had ended with promotion. Follow his profile for another way through this period: two promotion campaigns, relegation and a part in the Great Escape all belong to the same Albion career.

People · 2001–2006 at Albion

Darren Moore, standing tall.

A central figure in two promotions and the Great Escape.

Darren Moore arrived at The Hawthorns in September 2001. He made 116 appearances for Albion and helped the club win promotion in 2002 and again in 2004.

He was also part of the squad that survived in the Premier League in 2005. The club’s profile follows a relationship that continued through coaching and a later spell in charge of the first team. His history connects several chapters that can otherwise look like separate rises and falls.

Objects · 11 July 2003

A king at the gates.

The memorial that became a matchday meeting place.

The Jeff Astle Memorial Gates were unveiled on 11 July 2003, following discussion between his family, supporters and the club about how to celebrate his life.

The gates stand beside the Birmingham Road and honour Astle’s place in Albion history. Their design includes a crowned number nine and an image of his cup-winning celebration. The club’s account notes the artistic licence in showing that moment in home colours. This is a memorial shaped by memory, rather than a literal record of the shirt worn at Wembley.

Matches · 15 May 2005

The Great Escape.

Bottom at Christmas. Safe when it mattered.

Albion2–0Portsmouth

Albion began the final day of 2004/05 bottom of the Premier League. They needed to beat Portsmouth and depend on results elsewhere. After a goalless first half, Geoff Horsfield and Kieran Richardson scored the goals that gave Bryan Robson’s team a chance.

Norwich and Southampton lost, while Crystal Palace drew at Charlton. Albion survived, becoming the first Premier League side to stay up after being bottom at Christmas. It was a victory made meaningful by three other matches, and a final whistle followed by a wait for confirmation.

Matches · 4 May 2008

Champions, at Loftus Road.

A different division. Another trophy held aloft.

QPR0–2Albion

Albion’s 2007/08 campaign ended with the Championship title. On the final day at QPR, Kim Do-Heon and Chris Brunt scored in a 2–0 victory at Loftus Road.

The honour is distinct from the top-flight championship of 1920: the competition names changed, and the 2008 title was won in the second tier. Keeping that distinction clear helps place both achievements in their own footballing context. The club’s final-day retrospective gathers the moment alongside other promotion and survival days.

Matches · 22 July 2020

Promotion in a very different summer.

A 2–2 draw, empty stands and another return.

Albion2–2QPR

The delayed 2019/20 season reached its final round in July, after football’s interruption by the COVID-19 pandemic. Albion’s 2–2 home draw with QPR secured automatic promotion under Slaven Bilić.

Grady Diangana and Callum Robinson scored for Albion. Events elsewhere were important again, particularly Brentford’s result against Barnsley. The familiar tension of a promotion decider unfolded in the unfamiliar setting of football without supporters in the stands. It is a chapter in which the wider world is impossible to leave out of the match story.
